Concepts and terms

Source: vignettes/concepts.Rmd
concepts.Rmd

This is a short glossary of the words reprokit uses in its output. For worked examples see vignette("reprokit").

Why raw data stay the standard

Raw data let a reader do anything the author could do: check distributions and outliers, try another analysis, combine studies. Summary statistics allow only some of that. reprokit is for the cases where sharing raw data is genuinely not possible (for example because of consent or privacy rules). In those cases it states what readers lose, and the appendix records the reason you give (or says that none was stated), so that withholding data is never silent. reprokit never suggests a reason.

The verbs, in order

  1. Coverage table. coverage_table() lists which tests are covered, what each needs and what each leaves uncheckable.
  2. sufficient_stats(). Given a fitted result (or a formula with data and test), it gives the verdict, what to publish, what readers lose and the disclosure check, and stores the summaries at full precision. It accepts an lm, aov or chisq.test() result, a t.test() or cor.test() result with data, and for a mediation the two regressions.
  3. appendix(). Writes the appendix from those summaries. Underneath, it reproduces the result from the stored statistics alone and refuses if that does not match the original analysis (scaled difference below 1e-8). That round trip is why the statistics are called sufficient.

Readers use check_reported() with the test named first, for example check_reported("welch", ...).

Terms for authors

Sufficient set. The smallest set of numbers from which the whole result of a test can be recomputed exactly. For an independent-samples t-test: n, mean and SD of each group. For a Pearson correlation: n and r.

APA set. The numbers APA style conventionally asks authors to report for a test (for the independent t-test: n, M and SD per condition, t, df, p, d and a confidence interval).

Missing. The numbers in the sufficient set that the APA set does not contain. If a test has any, a paper that follows APA style does not give readers enough to reproduce the result. For the paired t-test the missing number is the correlation between the two conditions. appendix() prints these in block B.

Verdict. The outcome of sufficient_stats(): summaries_suffice, synthetic_possible or needs_raw_data (see verdicts()). A verdict is advice about what is enough; it is not a judgement on the author.

Verdict only. Version 0.1.0 stores statistics and checks reported numbers for the tests in coverage_table(). For other analyses (repeated-measures ANOVA, logistic and Poisson regression, SEM, rank tests, mixed models, GEE) sufficient_stats() gives a verdict and advice and nothing more.

Losses and reason. reprokit states what readers lose compared with the raw data, from the test (sufficient_stats(...)$lost, also printed). The reason for not sharing is the author’s own words, optional, and belongs to appendix() (sharing_reason). Without it the appendix says “not stated by the author”.

Choices. Decisions that the numbers do not reveal but the result depends on: one- or two-sided, confidence level, Student or Welch, and the effect-size convention (for example Cohen’s d with a pooled SD or Hedges’ g). The appendix asks you to declare them (block C); coverage_table() lists them per test.

Disclosure check. A check that the summaries do not single out a small group of people. With the default threshold of 5 it flags:

  • a group with fewer than 5 cases (t tests, one-way and factorial ANOVA);
  • a chi-squared cell (independence) or category (goodness of fit) with a count above 0 and below 5; empty cells are not flagged, because a zero count says that nobody is there;
  • a factor level with fewer than 5 rows in the fit (multiple and moderation regression, and any regression with a factor predictor), counted unweighted;
  • a total below twice the threshold (10), for every test.

For tests with no groups (one-sample and paired t, Pearson, simple mediation) the check is the total only, and the appendix says so. A flag makes sufficient_stats() return needs_raw_data.

The check is risk reduction, never a guarantee. Counts above the threshold can still identify someone (a rare combination known to a reader, or a summary that is close to one person’s data), and the check cannot know what a reader already knows. Passing it is not permission to share; a flag is a reason to share the raw data under controlled access or not at all.

Terms for readers

Rounding interval. A reported number stands for the range of values that round to it: “2.85” means 2.845 to 2.855. reprokit takes reported numbers as strings and checks against the whole interval. A reported “< .001” is the range 0 to .001. An interval is cut to the values the quantity can take (r lies between -1 and 1, p between 0 and 1).

Relation. A formula that links reported numbers, such as p from t and df. The check evaluates each relation whose inputs are reported and asks whether the reported output falls in the range the inputs allow.

Consistent / inconsistent. The numbers can, or cannot, all be correct as reported, after allowing for rounding and for the analysis choices. Inconsistent does not say which number is wrong, nor why. It does not say that the authors made a mistake.

Checkable / not checkable. A number is checkable if some relation connects it to other numbers. coverage_table() lists, per test, what is checkable and what is not, with the reason.

Coverage level. How much of the sufficient set the reported numbers cover, 0 to 3. Level 0: nothing could be checked. Level 1: internal coherence only (test statistic, df, p and CI against each other). Level 2: the test statistic was recomputed from the descriptives. Level 3: the whole sufficient set is reported. Level 3 is not itself a check; the checks are the comparisons in the table.

Status of a number. verified, coherent, inconsistent, unconfirmed, not reproducible or not checkable. See vignette("reprokit") for what each means.

Implied range. If a number needed by a relation is not reported, but the others constrain it, the range it must have been in. It is a derived value, not a claim that it was the true value.

Variant. One way of making the analysis choices (for instance Welch’s t, two-sided, 95%). The check tries all variants and keeps those that fit, with one shared choice per result. The values you pass to variants= are codes (such as "welch", "two.sided", "0.99"); the output prints readable labels for them (see ?check_reported).

What a check can and cannot tell you

A check can show that a set of reported numbers cannot all be right. It cannot show that they are right, that the analysis was appropriate, or which number is at fault. Where the answer is ambiguous, reprokit stays silent rather than flagging, because failing to check a correct paper is a limitation while flagging one is a false accusation.
